ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Measures adopted for Family Planning 
*281. SHRI MAN MOHAN SAMAL: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state : 
(a) whether Government have assessed the various family planning 
measures adopted by the third world and other developing countries in the 
world to control the population explosion; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have been planning to adopt a China like policy 
to control population in the country in near future; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof ? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (d) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) Government is aware of the measures adopted by the third 
world and other developing countries for population stabilization and sustainable 
development. A number of countries have implemented population programmes 
with the objective of empowering people to seek and accept services to fulfil 
their reproductive health goals and to seek other Reproductive Health Services. 
These have resulted in significant improvement in social development, and in 
the status of health and women's empowerment. These are reflected in better 
indicators and achievement with regard to Total Fertility Rate (TFR), Infant 
Mortality Rate (IMR) and Maternal Mortality Rate (MMR) which has eventually 
resulted in increased life expectancy at birth. The examples of countries which 
have achieved significant success in the programme are Thailand, Indonesia, 
Srilanka, Egypt, recently Iran and to some extent in Bangladesh.

RAJYA SABHA [10 December, 2001] 
(c) and (d) Government of India is signatory to the Plan of Action (POA) of 
International Conference or Popula tion and Development. The Chinese 
Population Policy is at variance with the Plan of Action of International 
Conference on Population and Develo pment. Recently approved National 
Population Policy of this country affirms Government's commitment towards 
voluntary and informed choice and c onsent of citizens while availing 
Reproductive and Child Health services and to continue the target free approach 
in administering family planning services. Considering the high unmet need for 
family planning services in the country, the Government's efforts are aimed at 
strengthening services, improving their quality and increasing outreach, and 
coverage through a series of strategies enumerated in the National Population 
Policy. 
SHRI MAN MOHAN SAMAL: Sir, the hon. Minister is aware of the fact 
that population problem is the biggest problem facing our country. It is 
undermining our economic growth rate. When countries like Indonesia and 
Egypt have achieved a significant success in controlling population, why is it 
that our country has failed to achieve this object? 
DR. C. P. THAKUR: Sir, I thank the hon. Member for asking this question. 
His question is the first in the List of Questions'. I congratulate him for that. Sir, 
this is a very burning problem facing our country. Today there are twelve questions 
on Health and Family Planning. That shows that the hon. Members are taking 
keen interest in the Department of Health and Family Welfare. I thank them for 
that also. Sir, every country has, according to its needs... 
SHRI SANGH PRIYA GAUTAM : Sir, last Friday on this very issue there 
was a discussion in the form of a Private Member's Bill. 
DR. C. P. THAKUR: Yes Sir, the Population Commission, headed by the 
Prime Minister, was constituted last year. Since then we have started taking very 
active measures to control population. Since some of the activists in the Rajya 
Sabha do not like the usage of the word 'control', I would use the word 
'stabilisation'. We are going ahead with it and, I think, the population of this 
country will be stabilised. 
SHRI MAN MOHAN SAMAL : Sir, I would like to know whether the 
Government proposes to take any hard measures in terms of both incentives and 
disincentives to be given to the people in order to address the population problem 
for safeguarding the national interest.

DR. C. P. THAKUR : Sir, the question, whether hard measures should be 
adopted or not, has been repeatedly discussed. It was the consensus of all the 
important members of the Population Commission that since hard measures 
were taken once and they were not ve ry successful, we should do it through 
more of services and a motivational approach. This approach has started paying 
dividends and the fertility rate has started coming down.

Sub-therapeutic drug formulations 
*287. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHAR YA: Will the MINISTER OF 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that many substandard sub-therapeutic 
drug formulations are available in the market and vast rural market is flooded 
with this; 
(b) if so, whether some effective measures are being planned to prevent 
marketing of such drug formulations; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof ? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) Gove rnment has received some complaints about sub-
standard and sub-therapeutic drugs being circulated in the market. 
Under the provisions of Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules 
thereunder, State Governments have been empowered to enforce the quality of 
drugs, including monitoring of manufacture, sale and distribution of drugs. The 
enforcement of quality control of drugs and pharmaceuticals is regulated by a 
system of licensing by the State Go vernments. The drugs control officers 
randomly draw samples from manufacturers, traders and get their quality validated 
through their Government labs. State Governments are required to take punitive 
actions, including launching of prosecution against the manufacturers or 
distributors who are found dealing in manufacture and sale of drugs of 
questionable quality, including sub-standard or sub-therapeutic formulations. 
In order to combat proliferation of drug formulations, the Central 
Government issued directions in November, 2000 under Section 33P to all the 
State Governments to instruct their licensing authorities not to issue licences for 
any new drug formulation, which includes new combination formulations of 
such drugs. Corresponding rules (69 & 71) under this Act are also being amended 
so as to ensure that no State Licensing Authority approves a new drug 
formulation at their level until such time it has been evaluated and approved by 
the Drugs Controller General of India. A Notification has already been issued on 
19-10-2001 inviting objections and suggestions. 
Provision related to Good Manufacturing Practices under Schedule M of 
the Act are also been upgraded and the amendment will be finally made shortly. 
24 

[10 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
The Central Government has also been advising the State Governments 
from time to time to provide adequate enforcement machinery; to establish their 
own State level drug testing facilities to ensure speedy analysis of drugs samples; 
to adopt cautious approach while approving licences for drug products which 
are sub-therapeutic, harmful or irrationa l; surveillance of suspected dealers; 
implementation of Good Manufacturing Practices (GMPs) are laid under Schedule 
M by the licensed manufacturers; cooperation of pharmaceuticals industry by 
regular interaction with them; collection of survey samples under National Survey 
Quality Evaluation of Drug Programme (NSQED); constitution/reactivation of 
State Drug Advisory Committee in which various trade and industry association 
as well as consumer associations should find representation. State Governments 
are being regularly assisted by providings funds and equipment for their 
laboratories; and by training of their lab and regulatory staff. 
Through the process of screening, manufacture and sale of 72 categories 
of drugs, including Fixed Dose Combinations (FDCs), have so far been phased 
out or prohibited. 
As far as quality is concerned, as per the information available from the 
State Licensing Authorities, out of 35570 samples tested during the period 
1999-2000,3666 were reported to be of sub-standard quality.

Spread of Small Pox by Bio-terrorists 
2133. SHRI H.K.JAVARE GOWDA: 
PROF. A. LAKSHMISAGAR: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state :  
(a) whether it is a fact that there is likelihood of the spread of small pox in 
the country by bio-terrorists after anthrax; and 
(b)if so, the preventive measures taken by Government in this regard 
? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) and (b) Not a single specimen tested for Anthrax in the 
designated laboratories found positive. There is a remote possibility of 
spread of small pox by the bio-terrorists. A detailed list of biological agents 
used as weapon prepared by the Indian Council of Medical Research along 
with signs and symptoms, likely method of dissemination, incubation period, 
lethality, and the availability of v accines, anti-microbial therapy and 
treatment has been circulated to Health Secretary and Director of Health 
Services of all States/UTs, and Central Government Hospitals advising them 
to take precautionary steps : 
(i) earmarking of maximum number of beds for emergency contingency. 
53 

RAJYA SABHA [ 10 December, 2001 ] 
(ii) stocking of vaccinces/sera/drugs to the extent possible. 
(iii) setting up a special team of doctors for coordinated action. They 
should be sensitized on the impact of such weapons and treatment 
measures. 
As per the WHO guidelines, the best method of stopping a small pox 
outbreak if occurs, is search and containment. Vaccination of entire population 
is not recommended since there is a risk  of severe reaction to the vaccine 
including death.

Supply of sub-standard contraceptives in U. P. 
2149.SHRIRAMAMUNIREDDYSIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state : 
(a) whether it has been revealed in the report of Comptroller and Auditor 
General of India that sub-standard contraceptives were supplied in U. P. ; 
(b) whether it was due to this that the birth rate in the State could not be 
controlled and the targets fixed under National Family Welfare Programme were 
not achieved ; and 
(c) the steps being taken to ensure that population explosion is checked, 
particularly in UP and Bihar ? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. 
THAKUR) : (a) Yes, Sir. The Report of  Comptroller and Auditor General of 
lndia, for the year ending March 2000, had made such observations. During the 
period, the supplies of contraceptives were made on the basis of norms which 
prescribe that at the lime of offering for inspection, the stocks offered for 
inspection should not have crossed more than 1/6 th of the total life, and should 
have a total shelf life not less than four years (48 months) from the date of 
manufacture. 
In addition, the contraceptives being supplied are meticulously tested 
first at the manufacturers' end and thereafter at designated laboratories authorized 
by the Government. A network of Regional Directors at field level are authorized 
to conduct field tests (alsoknown as Stage-II test) of supplies on a random 
basis. 
The States are fully authorized to return the stocks if these are found sub-
standard or of short expiry within a month of such instances coming to their 
notice. In such cases, the replacement of the quantity is to be made by the 
70 

[ 10 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
manufacturers/suppliers at their cost. However, during the period under 
report, no such references have been made by the Government of Uttar 
Pradesh. 
(b) No, Sir. Since 1st April 1996, the Family Welfare Programme is 
being  implemented all over India on the basis of Target Free Approach. The 
demand of the community for quality services is the driving force behind the 
programme making it people's programme. It is now called Community Needs 
Assessment Approach (CNAA). Therefore, no targets were fixed for Uttar 
Pradesh. 
(c) The Government of India has already adopted the comprehensive 
National Population Policy, 2000 that has brought in an integrated approach 
to reproductive and child health. The following measures are taken up to 
bring down birth rale which is already in the declining trend :— 
(i) An integrated and comprehensive programme of Reproductive and 
Child Health, which includes Maternal Health, Child Health and 
Contraception. 
(ii) Publicity of family planning methods, which include sterilization 
both for male and female, spacing methods namely, IUD insertions, 
oral pills and condoms. 
(iii) Fulfilment of unmet needs of contraception through provision of 
integrated service delivery at village levels. 
(iv) No Scalpel Vasectomy (NSV), wh ich is considered safe, simple and 
painless procedure of vasectomy, is being popularized to ensure 
male participation. 
(v) Information. Education and Communication Programme to create 
awareness about the benefit of small family. 
(vi)  Provision of additional inputs in weaker States/Districts. 
(vii) Inclusion of diverse health care providers. 
(viii) Community based social marketing of contraceptives. 
(ix) Focused attention is being given to eight demographically weak 
States namely Uttar Prradesh, Uttaranchal, Rajasthan, Madhya 
Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Bihar, Jharkhand and Orissa by creating an 
Empowered Action Group in the Department of Family Welfare to

Guidelines for approval of Bio-equivalence Centre 
2156. MISS MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there ar e no guidelines for approval of bio-
equivalence centres; 
(b) if so, how the approvals are being granted by the Drug Controller; and 
(c) whether the Drug Controller-General of India is accepting study reports 
from Centres which have no approval and when do they propose to come out 
with guidelines? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. 
THAKUR): (a) to (c) Bio availability is the process by which the drug is released 
from the oral dosage form and moves to the site of action. Bioavailability data 
provides an estimate of the fraction of the drug absorbed as well as its subsequent 
distribution and elimination. 
Under the provisions of the Drug and Cosmetics Rules, there is no specific 
statutory requirement for approval of centres/laboratories which undertake bio-
availability or bioeqvalence studies. However, there are internationally accepted 
norms about the facilities which are required to undertake such studies, the 
79 

RAJYA SABHA [10 December, 2001] 
protocols required to be followed and the manner in which studies need to be 
conducted including the ethical norms. 
Since data on bioavailability/bioequivalence is required to be furnished 
along with application for approval of New Drugs as per Schedule Y of the 
Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, the facilities and expertise available with such centres/ 
laboratories is now being ascertained through experts, and on satisfactory reports, 
such centres are being approved for the purpose of acceptance of bioequivalence 
studies conducted by them. 
Normally, bioavailability studies are being conducted by the departments 
of pharmacology in major medical institutions, some pharmacy colleges, in-
house R&D centres of few pharma industry and private research laboratories. 
Guidelines about the infrastructural requirements and working norms for 
bioequivalence studies are under preparation for consideration of the Drug 
Technical Advisory Board (DTAB). Steps are also being taken to assess the 
laboratories/centres which have been conducting these studies since earlier 
period.

such serious problem? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR.C. P.THAKUR):

pharmaceuticals to a product patent regi me cannot be gauged as there are no

drugs which may be used for treating life threatening diseases. 
The Joint Select Committee of Parliament is presently examining the

Flourishing spurious drugs trade 
2165. SHRI KRISHNA KUMAR BIRLA: Will the Minister of HEALTH . 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether due to lack in coordination between Government and State 
Governments the trade of spurious drugs is flourishing in the country; 
(b) if so, whether the spurious drugs manufactured in a particular State is 
sold in other States resulting in confusion for the authorities to take any action; 
(c) if so, whether Government propose to prepare any concrete action plan 
to check sale or manufacture of spurious drugs throughout the country; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR.C. P.THAKUR): 
(a) and (b) Manufacture and sale of spurious medicines is a clandestine activity 
indulged in by some unscrupulous and anti-social persons. 
Under the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules 
made thereunder, a drug manufactured in one state by licensed firms can be sold 
or distributed in other States. 
Government has been advising to Slate Governments from time to time to 
gear up their enforcement machinery to detect and unearth spurious/fake drugs 
moving in the inter-state commerce as we ll as speedy analysis of samples of 
drugs by their testing laboratories and to coordinate activities with other States. 
(c) and (d) The Drugs Controller General (India) has advised the State 
Drugs Controllers to take the following measures for curbing the incidence of 
spurious drugs : 
89 

RAJYA SABHA   [10 December, 2001]  
(i)      Constitution/reactivation of State Drug Advisory Committees in 
which various trade and industry associations as well as consumer 
associations should find representation,  
(ii)     Establishment of separate intelligenee-eum-legal machinery with 
police assistance,  
(iii)    Training to be provided to selected officials of Drug Control 
Administration in the modalities of intelligence work, prosecution 
etc. in respect of spurious/counterfeit drugs, 
(iv)    To ensure speedy analysis of drug samples by establishing own 
state level drug testing facilities, 
(v)     State Drugs Control Authorities to be cautious while approving 
licenses for drug products to ensure that 'look-alike' products are 
not encouraged,  
(vi)    To develop efficient communication facilities and recall procedures, 
(vii)   To undertake surveillance of suspected dealers,  
(viii) To engage experienced counsel for fighting spurious drug cases, 
(ix)     To obtain cooperation of Pharmaceutical industry by regular 
interaction with them.  
(x)      To collect Survey samples under National Survey Quality Evaluation 
of Drug (NSQED) programme. In addition, the 
following steps have also been taken : 
(1) Association of Pharmaceutical Industry and All India Organisation 
of Chemists and Druggists have been asked to take necessary initiative 
to collectively combat the menace of spurious drugs. 
(2) The problem of manufacture and sale of spurious drugs and the need 
to ensure its checking has been specifically explained to State Health 
Ministers during the meeting of Central Council of Health and Family 
Welfare held on 1th& 13th July, 2001 in New Delhi. 
(3) Ministry of Health and FW has constituted a Committee under the 
chairmanship of DGHS on July 18, 2001 associating members from 
industry, trade, drug regulatory officials and public representative to 
go into all aspects of the men ace of spurious drugs and suggest 
remedial measures.

the Central Government has undertaken a project to provide computer

Drug Testing Laboratories.

Spread of Dengue 
2170. PROF. M. SANK/ RALINGAM : Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state :—  
(a) whether dengue has recently raised its ugly head not only in Delhi 
but in Chennai and Tamil Nadu; 
(b) the preventive measures taken by Government to prevent spreading 
of this disease during the last year as well as current year; , 
(c) the reasons for spread of dengue in Tamil Nadu; and 
(d) the steps taken to treat dengue in Chennai and Tamil Nadu and 
prevent its spread in other parts of the country ? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C. P. 
THAKUR) : (a) to (d) There has been no  increase in Dengue cases in Delhi 
during the current year as  compared to the last year. However, increase in 
number of Dengue cases and deaths in Tamil Nadu has been recorded during 
the current year as against those during the last year. 
Increasing incidence of dengue in Chennai has been due to heavy rain 
in the month of September, 2001, resulting in creation of additional breeding 
habitats for the aedes aegypti mosquitos which spread the disease. 
Steps taken for control of dengue by the Government of Tamil Nadu 
and the Central Government include:—  
* Dengu/Dengue Haemorrhagie Fever (DHF) has been made a 
notifiable disease in Delhi. 
* Disease and vector surveillance. 
* Vector control mainly through source reduction. 
* Early diagnosis and case management in hospitals. 
* Information, Education and Communication For community   
awareness. 
* Early response to epidemics. 
* Regular monitoring and review of Dengue situation by the 
concerned authorities. 
* Deployment of domestic breading checkers for vector surveillance, 
source reduction and community education. 
* Enactment of legislative measures by MCD providing imposition of 
fine for abetting mosquitogenic conditions. 
98

* Development and issue of guidelines to States for prevention and control 
of Dengue/DHF and containment of outbreaks. 
* A control Room has been established at the Directorate of Natinal Anti

and providing technical guidelines to the States reporting incidence of 
Dengue.

statutory warning 'Cigarettes smoking is injurious to health' on all packages of 
Cigarettes and in all advertisements. The State Government/U.Ts. have been

inter-alia, include ban on all forms of advertisements in respect of all tobacco

sale of tobacco products to persons below the age of 18 years.

2181. SHRI K.RAMAMOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of HEALTH

Court in electron c and print media so that the general public are aware that

Indecent scenes shown in the films  
†2194. SHRIMATI SA ROJ DUBEY: Will the Minister of 
INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that despite the presence of Film Censor 
Board, indecent scenes are still shown in many films; 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to take other effective steps to 
check the picturisation of indecent scenes in the films; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor ? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING 
(SHRIMATI SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (d) In terms of the provisions contained 
in the Cinematograph Act, 1952, no film can be released for public exhibition 
unless it has been certified by the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC).

or molestation etc. in films. With a view to ensuring exhibition of a film only in its 
certified form, CBFC has hired, on a test case basis, a private detective agency, 
to carry Qtti regular checks in theatres in the four metropolitan cities, and report 
cases to violation to the concerned State authorities for prompt investigation 
and possible prosecution.

Speedy, economical and fair justice to common man 
2218. SHRI KR1PAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of LAW, JUSTICE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state : 
(a) whether he is aware that eye witnesses turn hostile from their testimony 
before the judge in the court due to money and influence; 
(b) if so, whether it is a fact, that taking undue advantage of provisions of 
Indian Criminal Procedure Code, Lawyers get engaged in saving the accused by 
unfair means instead of helping the court to get to the root of the truth ; and 
(c) if so, what reforms Government are contemplating for speedy, 
economical and fair justice to the common people of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF LAW. JUSTICE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
ARUN J AITLEY): (a) and (b) The Law Commission of India in their 154th Report 
on the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 has recommended, inter-alm insertion 
of a new sub-section, 1(A), in section 164 to read as follows : 
145 
 

RAJYA SABHA [ 10 December, 2001 ] 
"Every Investigating Officer shall send to the nearest Magistrate all material 
witnesses during the course of investigation and the Magistrate on oath record 
their statements, if such Magistrate is empowered to take cognizance of the case 
on police report. He shall keep such statements alongwith the FIR received by 
him and await the further police report under section 173. If he is not empowered 
to take such cognizance, he shall send the statements thus recorded on oath to 
the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of the case." 
In regard to a specific time-frame for a decision on the above, the 
Government has to take a view of the recommendations of the Law Commission 
in the 154th Report in entirety. 
(c) Government has proposed various remedial measures to provide fast, 
cost effective and fair justice to the countrymen. These include amendment of 
Civil Procedure Code and the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Code of Civil 
Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 2000 and the Code of Criminal Procedure 
(Amendment) Bill, 1994 are pending consid eration of Parliament. Further as 
regards Criminal Procedure Code and the Indian Penal Code, the Law Commission 
of India has comprehensively reviewed both the Acts. 
Further measures taken for speedy and cost effective justice are to increase 
the number of posts of Judges/Judicial Officers, establishment of Special Courts/ 
Tribunals and adoption of alternative modes of dispute resolution, such as 
arbitration and conciliation. Lok Adalats have been given a statutory base as 
supplementary forum for resolution of disputes. By March, 2001 the Lok Adalats 
have disposed of 1.67 crore (approx.) cases in the country.

Non-inclussion of some castesin the  list of OBCs 
2235. SHRI MAN MOHAN SAMAL: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased 
to state : 
(a) whether it is a fact that some castes in Orissa have not been included in 
the OBC category in the Centre's list where the State Government has declared 
the same caste as backward; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that some castes with equal status and origin 
from Orissa have been included in the Centre's list; and 
(d) if so, whether Government have assessed the social implications of 
this injustice, which has divided the people on caste lines, creating socio-cultural 
and other problems in future? 
THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT (DR. 
SATYANARAYAN JA TIYA): (a) Certain caste s/communities, which are 
declared as backward by the State Go vernment of Orissa, have not been 
included in the Central Lists of Backward Classes for Orissa. 
(b) to (d) The Supreme Court in its judgment in the case of Indira Sawhney 
and others vs. Union of India and others directed the Government of India, each 
of the State Government and the Administrations of Union Territories to 
constitute a permanent body for examining requests for inclusion and complaints 
of over-inclusion and under-inclusion of backward classes in the respective 
lists of OBCs. These bodies (Commissions) function independently and have 
their own procedure for examining the requests for inclusion of castes/sub-
castes in the lists of Backward Classes. 
Accordingly, the National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC) has 
been set up under the National Commission for Backward Classes Act, 1993 
which examines requests for inclusion of any class of citizen as a backward class 
in the lists and hears complaints of over-inclusion or under-inclusion of any 
backward class in such lists and tenders such advice to the Central Government, 
as it deems appropriate. The Commissi on has formulated guidelines for 
consideration of requests which include criteria covering social, educational 
167 

RAJYA SABHA   [10 December, 2001]  
and economic aspects of backwardness. The Commission also considers the 
views of the respective State Governme nt and the representatives of other 
interested parties before recommending any caste/community for inclusion in 
the Central Lists of OBCs or otherwise. Only those communities, which fulfil the 
above criteria are recommended by the NCBC for inclusion in the Central Lists 
of OBCs. The Government of India decides cases for inclusion/amendment in 
the Central Lists of Backward Classes on the basis of advice tendered by 
NCBC 
In the first phase, the castes/communities were included in the Central 
Lists of OBCs on the basis of commonality i.e., the castes/communities which 
were found common both in the Mandal Commission Report and State/UT list 
of backward classes. Thereafter, the cases of inclusion/amendment in the 
Central Lists of OBCs have been recommended by the NCBC. After thorough 
examination of each case in the light of procedure laid down by the Commission. 
Therefore, the question of injustice to any community does not arise.

Statement-I 
Schemes/Programmes implemented by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs for the 
welfare and development of Scheduled Tribes 
1. Special Central Assistance to Tribal Sub-Plan. (Central Sector Scheme)   . 
The main instrument of achieving Constitutional objectives of welfare and 
development of Scheduled Tribes is the Tribal Sub-plan which is implemented 
through 194 Integrated Tribal Development Projects (ITDPs), 259 pockets of 
Modified Area Development Approach (MADA) and 82 Clusters in 23 Tribal 
Sub-Plan State/Union Territories. 
Special Central Assistance is an important component of flow of funds for 
Tribal for Sub-Plan that is made available to State on the basis of a set criteria. 
The Special Central Assistant (SCA) is given by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs to 
the 20 Tribal Sub-Plan States/UT Administrations including North Eastern States 
of Assam, Manipur and Tripura as an additive to their own outlay to fill in the 
gaps. These grants are basically meant for family oriented income generating 
schemes in the sectors of agriculture, horticulture, minor irrigation, soil 
conservation, animal husbandry, forests,  education, cooperatives, fisheries, 
village and small scale industries and minimum needs programme. SCA is to be 
utilized in conjunction with TSP flow to meet the gaps which have not otherwise 
been taken care of by the State Plan. 
2. Grants under First Proviso to Article 275(1) of the Constitution  
The Ministry of Tribal Affairs provide grants to 18 Tribal Sub-Plan and 4 
tribal majority States under Firts Proviso to article 275(1) of the Constitution to 
meet the cost of such projects for tribal development as may be undertaken by 
the State Governments for raising the level of administration of the Scheduled 
Areas therein to that of the rest of the State. 
3. Girls Hostels for Scheduled Tr ibes. (Centrally Sponsored Scheme) 
The Scheme of Girls Hostels is a useful instrument for spreading education 
among ST Girls, under the scheme, Central assistance is given to States/UTs for 
construction of new hostel huildings and/or extension of existing hostels. This 
is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme where the cost of the construction of the 
hostels, building and/or extension of existing hostels, and the cost is equally 
shared between the Centre and the State in ratio of 50 : 50. In case of UTs, the 
Central Government bears the entire cost of the building, maintenance of the 
hostel is the responsibility of the concerned States/UTs. 
180 

[ 10 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
4. Boys Hostels for Scheduled Tribes. (Centrally Sponsored Scheme) 
The objective, terms and conditions as well as the pattern of assistance of 
this Scheme are same as that of the scheme for Girls Hostels." 
5. Establishment of Ashram School in Tribal Sub-Plan Area. (Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme) 
The Scheme of Ashram School was launched in 1990-91 with the objective 
to extend educational facilities like establishment of residential schools for STs 
in an environment conducive to learning. The funding for the Scheme with the 
State is done on matching (50:50) basis, while cent per cent assistance is given 
toUTs. 
The central assistance is mainly for construction of Ashram School 
buildings, hostels and staff quarters. The expenditure on the maintenance is met 
by the concerned State/UT. The scheme covers primary, secondary and senior 
secondary level of education. 
6. Grant in aid for Voluntary Organisation working for the welfare of 
STs. (Central Sector Scheme) 
Numerous important projects are being implemented by the Ministry of 
Tribal Affairs through voluntary organizations which are working for the welfare 
of the Scheduled Tribes. A wide spectrum of projects, which are of direct benefit 
to the tribals are considered under this scheme. The projects include residential 
schools, hostels, medical mobile dispensaries, computer training units, shorthand 
and typing training units, Balwadies/creches (in areas not covered by the ICDS 
programme) libraries and audio-visual units for dissemination of vital information 
relevant to the welfare of Scheduled Tribes. The grant is generally restricted to 
90% of the approved total cost of the project, the balance 10% is borne by the 
voluntry organizations. 
7. Research and Training  
(a)     Grant to Tribal Research Institute 
Tribal Research Institute have been set up in 14 States. These Institutes 
are involved in conducting research and evaluation studies, seminars, workshops 
on various subjects relevant to tribals, provide training and orientation to State 
Government officials and to give support to State Government for preparation of 
Tribal Sub-Plans. Most of the Institutes are also having tribal museums for 
exhibition of tribal artifacts. Under the scheme, grants are given on 50 :50 basis 
to States for running and maintaining these Institutes. 
181 

 
RAJYA SABHA [ 10 December, 2001 ] 
(b) Supporting Project of All-India or Inter-State nature (Scheduled Tribes) 
The scheme relating to grant for research and evaluation projects. Grants 
up to Rs. 2.50 lakhs per project for period of 8-12 months are given to Non-
Governmental Organizations, Government institutions and Universities who 
conduct research/evaluation studies. 
(c) Award of Research Fellowship in various aspects of Tribal Development 
(Doctoral/Post Doctoral Fellowship) 
Grants are given for Research Fellowship on 100% basis to students/ 
scholars, who are registered with a University for working on tribal development 
programmes/problems. The rates of fellowship for doctoral and post doctoral 
courses are Rs. 2800/- and Rs. 3200/- per month respectively. In addition an 
annual contingency grant of Rs. 10000/- is allowed. 
8. Share Capital Contribution to TRIFED 
Tribal Cooperative Marketing Development Federation of India Limited 
(TRIFED) was set up by the Government of India, in the year 1987, with the prime 
objective of providing marketing assistance and remunerative prices to 
Scheduled Tribes Communities for their minor forest produce and surplus 
agricultural produce and to wean them away from exploitative private traders 
and middlemen. 
The authorized share capital of TRIFED is Rs. 100.00 crores and the paid 
up capital has gone upto Rs. 99.73 crores out of which Government of India's 
contribution is Rs. 99.50 crores. 
9. Price Support to TRIFED  
The price of Minor Forest Produce (MFP) and Surplus Agriculture Produce 
(SAP) are subject to fluctuations. For meeting the unforeseen contingencies of 
losses because of such fluctuations in the prices and ensure remunerative prices 
to the tribal farmers for their produce, the Ministry has been giving financial 
Assistance to the TRIFED to set off part of such losses. 
10. Grant in aid to State Tribal Development Cooperative Corporations for 
Minor Forest Produce 
Minor Forest Produce (MFP) is an important source of earning for tribals. 
Most of the States have set up Tribal Development Cooperative Corporations, 
Minor Forest Produce Trade and Development Federations or Forest Development 
Corporation for dealing with Minor Forest Produce items. Grants given under 
182 

[ 10 December, 2001 ] RAJYA S ABH A 
this Scheme can be utilized by the State for (i) strengthening the share capital base 
of TDCCS for increasing the volume of prcurement of MFPs; (ii) constructions of 
scientific warehouses; (iii) establishing process industries for value addition to 
MFP items; and (iv) research and development activities by the Corporation. 
11. Educational Compex in Low Literacy Pockets for Development of ST 
Girls in Tribal Areas. (Central Sector Scheme) 
The Scheme was introduced in 1993-94 for improving literacy among ST 
women in district with less than 10% literacy, and implemented through Non-
Governmental Organizations/Organizations or institutes set up by Government as 
autonomous bodies/educational and other institutions like Local Bodies and 
Cooperative Societies. A total of 136 Districts of 11 States are covered under the 
scheme. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs pr ovides full assistance for setting up of i 
the educational complexes. A complex is meant for girls studying in class I to V 
with a strength of 30 girls in every class with a provision for training in craft/ 
vocational education. Food and lodging is free for the students. There is a 
provision for supply of two sets of uniforms per year per student, free periodical 
medical check-ups for the children and adult education for the parents of the girls 
in the evening. An incentive of Rs. 50 per student per monUi is to be paid to the 
partents for sending their daughters to these educational complexes. 
12. Vocational Training in Tribal Areas (Central Sector Scheme) 
The main aim of this scheme is to develop the skill of the tribal youth in 
order to gain employment/self employment opportunities. This scheme is 
implemented through the State Governments/UT Administrations, Institutions or 
Organisations set up by Government as  autonomous body, educational and other 
institutions like local bodies and cooperative societies and Non-Governmental 
Organisations. Each center may cater to five vocational courses in traditional skills 
depending upon the employment potential of the area. Each tribal boy/girl will be 
trained in two trades of his/her choice, the course in each trade being for a duration 
of three months. Each trainee will be attached at the end of six months to a Master 
Craftsman in a semi-urban/urban area for a period of six months to learn his skill by 
practical experience. There is provision for monthly stipend and grant for raw 
material for the trainees. 
13. Village Grain Bank (Central Sector Scheme) 
As a part of Government efforts to prevent deaths of children in remote and 
backward tribal areas due to fall in nutrition standards, a scheme of Village 
183 

RAJYA SABHA [ 10 December, 2001 ] 
Grain Banks has been launched during 1996-97. A one time grant towards 
purchase of grains, at the rate of 1 quintal per family of tribals in such areas, 
storage facilities for the grains and purchase of weights and scales is provided 
by the Ministry of Tribal Affairs through TRIFED, as the channelising agency. 
The Grain Bank is to be managed by the village committee elected by the 
beneficiaries themselves who as members of the bank can borrow grains from 
the Grain Banks at the times of scarcity. 
14.    Development of Primitive Tribal Groups (Central Sector Scheme) 
There are certain tribal communities who are having a low level of litracy, 
declining or stagnant population, pre-agricultural level of technology and are 
economically backward. 75 such groups have been identified and have been 
categorized as Primitive Tribal Groups (PTGs). Their problems and needs are 
different from other Scheduled Tribes. As Primitive Tribal Groups constitute the 
most vulnerable among the STs, and prio rity needs to be accorded for their 
protection and development, scheme has been started during 1998-99 for their 
development. 
Under this scheme funds are made available for those items/activities, 
which though very crucial for the survival, protection and development of PTGs 
are not catered to by any existing scheme. 
*15. Post-Ma trie Scholarship for Sc heduled Tribes Students (Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme) 
The objective of the scheme is to provide fianancial assistance to students 
belonging to Scheduled Tribes pursuing post-Matriculation recognized courses 
in recognized institutions. The scheme covers professional, technical as well as 
non-professional and non-technical courses at various levels and the scheme 
also includes correspond ence courses including distance and continuing 
education. The scheme is implemented by the State Governments and UT 
Administrations, which receive 100% Central assistance over and above the 
committed liability which is required to be borne by them from their own budgetary 
provisions. The committed liability is equal to the expenditure reached in the last 
year of the preceding Plan period. Th e requirement of committed liability of 
North Eastern States has been dispensed with from 1997-98. 
The value of the existing scholarship includes maintenance allowance, 
reader charges for blind students, study tour charges, thesis typing/printing 
charges, book allowance to students pursuing correspondence courses and 
compulsory non-refundable fees charged by the educational institutions. 
184 

[ 10 December, 2001 ] RAJ YA S ABH A 
* 16.  National Overseas Scholarship Scheme for Scheduled Tribes (Non-Plan) 
The Scheme provides for financial assistance to meritorious students for 
pursuing higher studies abroad in specified fields of Master level courses, Ph.D 
and Post Doctoral research programmes, in the field of Engineering, Technology 
and Science for Scheduled Tribes, Denotified, Nomadic and Semi-nomadic tribes. 
The selected candidates are provided the cost of tuition and other educational 
fees charged by the foreign University etc., maintenance and other grants along 
with travel expenses. In addition passage grants are also available to candidates 
belonging to ST. who are in receipt of merit scholarship for post graduate studies, 
research or training abroad (excluding attending seminars, workshops, 
conferences) from a foreign government/organization or under any other scheme 
where cost of passage is not provided. 
17. Grants under second proviso to Article 275(1) of the Constitution (Non-
Plan) 
Fixed grant is given to the Government of Assam in respect of the 
administration of tribal areas in Hill districts of North Cachar and Karbi Anglong. 
* 18.  Coaching & Allied Scheme for STs (Centrally Sponsored Scheme) 
Under the scheme, free coaching facilities are provided to ST students 
through Pre-Examination training centres, to help them to compete in various 
competitive examinations having all-India recruitment character. The Pre-
Examination Training course for STs run by State Government/Universities/ 
Private Coaching Institutes will be eligible for assistance under the scheme. The 
scheme provides for stipends upto Rs. 500/- per month to the outstation students 
and Rs. 150/- per month for local students for taking coaching at the pre-
examination training centres. 
* 19.  Up gradation of Merit of ST Students (Central Sector Scheme) 
 The objective of the scheme is to upgrade the merit of ST students by 
providing them remedial and special coaching in classes IX to XII. While the-
remedical coaching aims at removing de ficiencies in various subjects, the 
special coaching is provided with a view to prepare the students for competitive 
examinations for seeking entry into professional courses like Engineering and 
Medical disciplines. The scheme provides for 100% central assistance to the 
States/UT's. A package grant of Rs. 15,000/- per student per year is provided 
and the State/UT's are not required to bear any financial burden. 
185 

RAJ YA S ABHA [ 10 December, 2001 ] 
*20.  Book Bank for Scheduled Tribes Students (Centrally Sponsored Scheme) 
The objective of the scheme is to provide books to deserving ST students 
pursuing Medical, Engineering, Agriculture, Veterinary, Polytechnics, Law, 
Chartered Accountancy, MBA and Bio-Science courses. The scheme provides 
for sharing of text-books by two students in respect of graduate level courses 
and separate set of books is provided to individual students at Post-Graduate 
level and for those pursuing Chartered Accountancy course. The Scheme is 
implemented by the States/UT's and the expenditure on the scheme is co-shared 
on 50 : 50 basis between the Centre and the State Governments. The U.T. 
administrations receive 100% Central Assistance. 
* 21. State Tribal Development Finance Corporation 
State Tribal Development Finance Co rporation act as guarantors and 
promoters providing margin money loans and subsidy to the target groups. 
They play useful role in the mobilisation of finances for economic development 
of Scheduled Tribe living below the poverty line. The State Corporations mainly 
take up employment oriented schemes in the areas of (i) Agriculture and allied 
sector, (ii) Minor Irrigation, (iii) Trades and Services, (iv) Transport and (v) Self-
Employment schemes. 
*The schemes were being operated both for SCs and STs by the Ministry of 
Social Justice and Empowerment. With the creation of the Ministry of Tribal 
Affairs, funds have been earmarked separately for the Ministry under these 
schemes from the year 2000-2001.

Need to enact law to avoid experiments on human beings 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIR EDDY (Andhra Pradesh)*: Sir, 
my Special Mention relates to the need to enact law to avoid experimentation 
on human beings. It is easy in India to conduct biomedical experiments on 
human beings than on animals because there is no law to regulate or control 
experiments on human beings. Recently , the Regional Cancer Centre in 
Kerala, conducted unethical trials of a banned drug, M4N, which had been 
smuggled in India, ip collaboration wi th the John Hopkins University of 
America, on 26 oral cancer patients,  without adequate preliminary tests on 
animals. There is a full-fledged law passed by Parliament to ensure 
monitoring of experiments on animals, but nothing for human beings. Are we 
not equal to guinea pigs even? There are only guidelines issued by the ICMR. 
This has given an elbow space, and is left to the conscience of researchers 
either to follow or flout the guidelines. I failed to understand as to why the 
Health Ministry failed to formulate the ethical guidelines for Biomedical 
Research on Human Subjects framed by the ICMR into law? Ironically, India, 
in 1980, was one of the first countries of  the world to take note of the ethical 
considerations for research on human be ings. In spite of this, we have not 
been able to enact any law in this regard. The ICMR has also recommended 
for the constitution of an Ethics Committ ee in all research institutions. But not 
even a single institution has constituted the same. The experiments carried 
out are nothing but human rights viol ation, and stringent action has to be 
taken on the violators. I request the Go vernment to immediately enact law to 
stop experiments on human beings.

"That the Bill further to amend the Passports Act, 1967, be

Madam, I am grateful to the hon. Member for his observations. His 
principal objection, as you pointed out, relates to the Ordinance and not to the 
Bill. His second objection relates to some  reports that have come to his notice 
about corruption in some Consulate. Ab out this particular aspect of issuance 
of passports, I would be very grateful if the hon. Member were to write to me 
and give me the details. I can assure him that we will attend to the issue very 
seriously.  We will take up every such instance very seriously. 
The Passports Act, 1967, vide Section 10, contains provisions for 
variation, impounding and revocation of passports and travel documents. 
However, there is no provision in this Act to prevent a person wanted for, or 
indulging in, criminal or anti-national activities, from leaving the country during 
the period when action to revoke or impound his/her passport is initiated and 
the passport is actually revoked or impounded. At present, the concerned 
security and enforcement agencies issue Look-Out-Circulars to prevent such 
persons from leaving the country, which are then acted upon by the 
emigration authorities. 
246 

RAJYA SABHA [10 December, 2001] 
I will now explain the reasons for the urgency of issuing an 
Ordinance. As a few Look-Out-Circulars were challenged in the courts, a need 
was felt for the introduction of a meas ure which would temporarily prevent a 
holder of a passport or a travel document  from leaving the country. Any action 
initiated by an authorised investigati ng or enforcement agency by issuing a 
Look-Out-Circular is to be simultaneously accompanied by a request to the 
Passport Authorities for variation, revocation or impounding of the passport, in 
accordance with the provisions of Section 10 of the Passports Act, 1967. 
In view of the urgency - there has  been an observation from the 
court; and this is what has lent an urgency to this- - to provide a legal basis for 
this, and to prevent the departure from the country of persons in respect of 
whom Look-Out-Circulars already exist, and whose activities were considered 
prejudicial to the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State or 
public order, the Passports (Amendment) Ordinance, 2001, was promulgated by 
the President on Tuesday, the 23 rd October, 2001. The proposed Passports 
(Amendment) Bill, 2001, proposes to replace this Ordinance. 
The proposed Bill would empower the representatives of the 
concerned raw enforcement as well as preventive agencies to initiate action

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Supply of Gasohol in the country 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI SURESH PACHOURI): Now, Shri Ram 
Naik to make a Statement. You can either  lay it on the Tabl e of the House or 
read it. 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): Sir, I would prefer reading i t. Sir, Brazil has been producing ethanol 
from sugarcane molasses and juice for more than 40 years. Similarly, U.S.A 
has also been producing it from corn-maize. Ethanol thus produced, is being 
blended in petrol to the extent of 20 per  cent to 24 per cent in Brazil, and is 
widely used, successfully, as auto-fuel. As per the present Bureau of Indian 
Standard specifications, ethanol content in petrol is permitted up to 5 per cent. 
Ethanol is produced from renewable source of energy, and by using 
it in the petroleum industry, the sugarc ane cultivation and industrial activity 
would stimulate higher growth in the primary as well as secondary sectors, 
apart from contributing to cleaner environment. In order to ascertain economic 
and operational aspects of bl ending of ethanol in petrol in terms of logistics, 
pricing, environmental impact, etc. in the Indian context, the Government had 
launched three Ethanol-Gasoline Pilot projects; two in Maharashtra and one in 
Uttar Pradesh, covering over 300 retail outlets, which have been selling 5 per 
cent ethanol-blended petrol. 
In addition to field trials being conducted through pilot projects, 
Research and Development studies are also being separately undertaken on 
various types of vehicles to monitor the impact of using Ethanol-petrol blends 
on driveability, fuel economy, vapour-l ocking etc. R and D studies would be 
completed by March 2002. 
Encouraged by the success of the pilot projects, I had convened two 
meetings, one on 12th November, 2001 with the representatives of the various 
Ministries, and the representatives of the State Governments of Maharashtra 
and U.P., and, subsequently, on 29th November, 2001 with my colleagues, the 
Minister of Agriculture, Shri Ajit Singh,  the Minister of Food, Consumer Affairs 
and Public Distribution, Shri Shanta Kumar, the Minister of 
295 

[10 December. 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
State for Petroleum and Natural Gas and Parliamentary Affairs, Shri Santosh 
Kumar Gangwar, the Minister of State for Rural Development, Shri 
Annasaheb M.K. Patil, Representatives of Governments of Uttar Pradesh and 
Maharashtra, along with members of the Task Force also attended the 
meetings. Various supportive actions from the Union and State Governments 
with regard to production and use of ethanol were also discussed. 
Based on these deliberations, Government have taken the following 
decisions: 
(i)  Sale of petrol blended with ethanol @ 5 per cent in the 
country to be implemented in two phases. During the first 
phase, States of Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Haryana, 
Karnataka, Maharashtra, Punjab, Tamil Nadu and Uttar 
Pradesh would be covered and during the second phase, 
rest of the country. 
(ii)   Existing three Pilot Projects to take up blending of Ethanol 
in Petrol @ 10% after sorting the issues such as 
modifications of BIS specifications, etc. 
(iii)  Rs.4 crores were sanctioned for R&D studies on blending of 
ethanol in diesel, keeping in view of the fact that about 80% 
of fuel consumed by automobiles in India is diesel. These 
studies are to be completed within 6 months. 
In order to encourage blending of  ethanol in petrol, it would be 
necessary to price it well below the import parity price of petrol. Sugar 
industries and distilleries would have to supply ethanol at competitive price. 
Further, Government have taken a major decision to amend the 
Sugar Development Act, 1982, so t hat production of ethanol and co-
generation of power from bagasse would get financial assistance from the 
Sugar Development Fund. This would give impetus to encourage our efforts in 
increasing the use of ethanol for blending and for an efficient use of the entire 
quantity of molasses currently produced. The increased returns to the units 
concerned would naturally flow back to the agriculturists. With stable and 
assured payments, the farmers would gain in the process. 
 
 
296 

RAJYA SABHA [10 December, 2001] 
I do hope that this decision of blending ethanol in petrol would usher 
a new era as it will benefit the country and especially sugarcane producing 
farmers and oil industry.   This decision would also help to save valuable  
foreign  exchange  as  the  country  is  importing  nearly  70%  of petroleum 
requirements.
